pages: Introduction

The Cabin In The Forest
The cabin door opened with a forceful
bang as the man with the thick mustache,
and the red haired woman returned
inside.
Drying blood covered their tattered
clothing as their chests heaved and
exhaled with exhaustion. Their weapons
— the man’s crossbow and the woman’s
rusting ax— were just as drenched with
blood as they were. The fear on their faces
reflected just as much as my own.
“A-are we gonna be ok?” I asked, barely
able to contain my tears.
The site of their dulling weapons was
almost as frightening as the creatures that
lurked just outside.

“Of course we are sweetie,
” came a
calming voice from behind me.
It was the old lady. She was my favorite of
everyone here. Her words were always so
gentle and reassuring. I could tell she’d
had a hard life, based on the scars across
her neck and the limp in her steps. That
didn’t seem to stop her from being a kind
person though.
“Most of ‘em wouldn’t be able to get in
anyway” she continued as she motioned
me towards her rocking chair near the
fireplace.
“Come on back over here, I’m
sure those two will do everything they can
to protect us from those things.
”
Maybe she was right.

“Elk crap!”
The man across from us yelled through a
twisted laugh.
He was a twisted man. The grayed hair on
his balding head fell long and thin,
hanging desperately down his broad
shoulders. His face was always pointing to
the old window next to his chair,
watching as if expecting any minute now
for something to reveal itself.
What was he looking for? Nothing could
be seen out of the window, nothing but
the thick violet fog that blanketed the
forest ...and its evils.
“I’ve been exploring these woods long
enough to know that nothing ever ends all
hunky dory,
” The old man’s dry remarks
continued as his eyes shifted slightly to
the two at the door.
“But hell, my knee’s been givin me
problems for quite a while now.

They’d probably be doing me a favor.
”
His wicked laugh once again sounded.
The old man was my least favorite out of
everyone. He was mean, always mocking
with his laugh, always staring.
I wish my dad was here, he’d stop the
man from being mean to me.
“No need to fret, child, we’ll be fine,
” said
the old woman as she reached for my
shaking hands. Her eyes cut angrily to the
old man. I don’t think she liked him
either.
“Alright, alright everyone. I suggest we all
take a moment to calm down.
” The man
with the thick mustache’s breathing
continued to labor as he spoke. I guess he
hadn’t caught his breath yet, him nor the
red haired lady. Their tired footsteps
thudded loudly against the wooden cabin
floors as they made their way to the
uncomfortable couch next to the old
woman’s rocking chair.

“Judging from the number of ‘em out
there, I’d say we’re gonna be hulled up
here all night.
” His legs kicked up lazily
atop the coffee table in front of him as he
placed his last three crossbow bolts
between himself and the woman with red
hair.
“The worst of them’s been taken care of,
and the ones still out there ain’t moving
without instruction. We might as well get
comfortable until mornin’
”
.
The woman’s face balled in anger, but
quickly returned to one of struggle as she
lay her head back and gasped for air. The
battle outside must’ve been extremely
hard, of course it would be.
“Get comfortable?” The old lady
questioned as she continued to hold my
hand.
“And how do you just expect us to do that?
We’re surrounded by the fog and all of
those creatures out there. Mornin ain’t till
at least four hours from now.
”

“I don’t know, ma’am,
” he continued with
more control of his breathing,
“ But I’d
rather see us all walk out of here with
sound minds and bodies. We can’t do that
if we’re fidgeting and causing a ruckus.
That’ll attract more of the bigger
creatures.
”
The old woman exhaled in agreement.
“I know how we can pass a few hours,
”
came an aged voice followed by a wicked
cackle.
“Times like these, a couple of good
stories tend to get your mind off things.
”
“Stories?” Echoed the red haired woman.
“Back when I was younger. Me and mine
would get in all kinds of binds. Through
all the long battles, hunger, scares, and
drunken nights we would always gather
round and spin a couple of yarns.
” He
grinned as he spoke.
”It was always…
good for morale.
”

For a while no one said anything. I guess
they were all just thinking it over, same as
me. A couple of stories didn’t sound bad
either. My dad would always tell me
stories when I was down.
“Well,
” started the thick mustached
man as he looked around the room,
not?”
“why
For a while no one said anything. I guess
they were all just thinking it over, same as
me. A couple of stories didn’t sound bad
either. My dad would always tell me
stories when I was down.
“Well,
” started the thick mustached
man as he looked around the room,
not?”
“why
He placed the crossbow from his lap to
the couch as he leaned forward towards
the old man.
“Why don’t you do us the
honor.
”
The old man grinned.

A Mother’s Warning
“Don’t go into the forest at night,
” my
mother used to always warn,
”There are
things there that bite and don’t let go.
”
I always listened to her, well most of the
time.
Other times I would wait at the outskirts
of our village until dusk, watching as the
eerie violet fog that surrounded the forest
darkened at the sun’s setting.
There were always strange sounds comin’
from within the forest; alluring sounds.
Sometimes I would get brave enough and
take a step or two into the fog to get a
closer listen– but only sometimes though.

Eventually, as I got older, I started packin’
a bag and going campin’ in the forest. I
mean, I just had to find the source of that
sound, right? And I wasn’t the only one
either.
Met some friends on one of the trips, so
now I wasn’t alone. They were kind of
slow, but the forest wasn’t as scary with
them around. We would walk together,
talk, and eat together.
However, this one particular time as we
all knelt together eating delicious meat
from some unfortunate bloody carcass, I
couldn’t get my mother’s words out of my
head. I wonder if this guy’s mother had
ever warned him about the dangers of the
forest. If so, then he really should’ve
listened.

The Cabin In The Forest 2
The gray haired man finished his story
with a sly glance at me as he laughed his
wicked laugh. The very sight of his
amused face and crooked teeth made my
skin crawl. Why was he so obnoxious?
“You horrid man,
” yelled the old lady
defensively as she held my hand.
“Are you
ok, child?”
“I’m fine.
”
My hand slipped carefully from hers. I
didn’t need to be shielded. I know all too
well what happens out there.
“Have you seen people turn into one of
those things before?”
The grayed man’s eyes glossed as he
turned his head thoughtfully towards the
fogged window.
“More than I care to
remember.
”

His tone had changed. For the first time of
the night, he seemed to get serious.
“It’s not something you ever forget… no
matter how many times you’ve seen it…
”
The room once again grew quiet, quiet
enough to bring attention to the crackling
fire wood in the pit. If you listened long
enough it kind of started to sound like the
faint growling of the things in the fog. Its
mesmerizing glow helped the time roll.
A while had passed before anyone said
anything. Everyone, just like me, was
probably thinking about lost loved ones.
I was the one to break the silence.
“Why a crossbow?”
“What do you mean?” the mustached man
asked.

“Why not a short bow? I’m sure ammo
would be easier to come across, right?
And doesn’t it get heavy while you're out
fighting?”
“Not particularly.
” He reached for his
weapon and motioned it towards me,
for yourself.
” He smiled.
“see
The sight of it up close sent chills through
my spine
“No… no thanks…
”
“Bad experience?”
“My dad… he was—
”
Before I could finish my sentence my
vision had begun to blur.
Stupid tears, why’d they have to start
falling now? I thought I had gotten past it.

The man’s eyes widened with sorrow.
“I’m sorry, little lady,
” he expressed as he
quickly and awkwardly hid the crossbow
under his garments.
“I didn’t kn—
“
“
—No, it’s fine. You didn’t know.
”
A moment of awkwardness filled the air.
“Well,
” began the old lady in a well
meaning tone,
“why don’t we tell
everyone a little more about ourselves.
”
The grayed man’s eyes cut to her. He
stood, suddenly— quicker than I thought
possible for him.
“You know we can’t do that. Are you
trying to get us killed?”
“N-no, I just—
”

“
—And here I was thinking that I was too
old to hear anymore stupid ideas in my
lifetime.
” He continued in growing anger.
“Would ya just listen all the way before
you blow up!?”
“Listen for what? More stupidity to
spew!?”
Their bickering continued. Funny, I was
sure everyone here were strangers yet
these two argued like a married couple.
They were both up now, full on yelling in
each other’s faces.
“Ok, ok enough!” The mustached man
finally interrupted as he stepped in
between them.
The red haired woman sat silently,
unbothered, admiring the rusting blade of
her ax. Not surprising. She didn’t seem
much for words, or people for that matter.
She’d probably be the first to leave at
daybreak.

The mustached man’s de-escalation
continued.
“Let’s all sit back down and
discuss it.
” Both parties went angrily to
their chairs. I couldn’t help but chuckle.
“Ok,
” he began again.
“Now obviously we
can’t tell each other our names, that’d be
like waving the dinner bell to those
creatures out there,
” he plopped on the
couch before finishing,
“however, we
should at least know a little something
more about each other. It’d help ease the
tension.
” He smiled warmly as he looked
at me and then to the old lady.
“Well, ma’am, where were you headed
before we ended up in this sorry
situation?”
The old lady’s head hung slightly at the
question. Her eyes seemed to water.
“Well… I was…
”

Her hands reached slowly for mine as she
gathered strength to finish.
“I was looking for my granddaughter, she
disappeared sometime ago,
”
her voice trembled slightly.
“It’s been so
long since I’ve seen her, and… I don’t
know how much longer I can bear the
thought of what might’ve happened to
her.
”
Her eyes dried quickly as she regained
her composure.
“She’d be about your age
now,
” she spoke as she looked into my
eyes. Her hands once again caressed my
own.
“I’m looking for someone too,
”
the grayed man interrupted as he once
again looked out into the violet fog. He
was horrible at reading the room, either
that or he didn’t care much. What an
inconsiderate man.
“Two someone’s
actually,
” his nose twitched slightly,
“A
pair of brothers…
”

He said nothing else, again reserving
himself to his own thoughts as he looked
out of the window.
“So the both of you have similar goals, I
”
see,
the mustached man exclaimed, picking up
the slack of conversation that the grayed
man had left.
“I wish that I could say that I was doing
something so selfless. That way if this
forest were the place where I met my
grave, I could at least die knowing that I
was doing something meaningful.
”
The look in his eyes grew distant; his
smile faded slightly.
“So, why are you here?” The old lady
asked.

He sighed.
“I was forced to leave my settlement after
a sickness swept through.
” His mouth
curled,
“now I’m just a wanderer looking
for a place to call home.
”
“Happens to the best of us,
” the old man
responded somberly as he continued to
stare out the window.
“Yea, well, I suppose it does.
”
The three nodded in agreement.
“And you?” the mustached man
questioned as he looked towards the red
haired woman. Everyone’s head turned.
“What brought you here?”

The woman exhaled loudly, preparing to
speak. Her eyes never left her rusted and
bloodied ax.
She spoke slowly.
“The scariest thing about the forest…
”

The Scariest Thing About The Forest
There are lots of good reasons to be
afraid of the forest. There are so many
reasons that it would be down right stupid
not to fear it. Missing people, violet fog,
eerie sounds, and strange creatures are
just a few; but none of these are the
scariest thing.
I’m sure you all know why, right? No?!
Well, where do I start?
Sure, people vanishing mysteriously in
the woods is creepy, but you can come up
with a few things to explain that.
Predators of all kinds are all around. As
sad as it is, who’s to say that those
unfortunate travelers didn’t just get
caught on the bad end of a grizzly’s
stomach. Of course that's the best case

The eerie sounds? Well, most people have
never heard a red elk’s call up close, or
the sound of a mountain lion’s roar. Of
course you’d fear them. But once ya find
out what it is, then it’s just that; hopefully.
The violet fog? Yes, now that is indeed
scary. Walkin’ corpses, body-snatchers,
creepin’ shadows, and who knows what
else is out there; but once ya learn its
patterns you can more or less avoid its
most dangerous parts all together.
All of these are scary in their own right,
but none of these is the scariest thing in
the forest. That title is reserved for the
tall, vine covered, monument of mystery
deep within; The Tower.

Yea, I know what you're thinkin’
.
“What’s so scary about a tower?”
Everything!
No one knows where the tower came
from, or who could have even built it for
that matter. Sure there are theories, but
none of them seem to hold up.
Countless people have gone out in
search of it, but none have returned. Yea,
that’s scary, but it gets even scarier when
you get The Call.
It comes to a person mysteriously and
suddenly— it doesn’t matter the age.
Some are unfortunate enough to be born
with it, some get it when they’re old, some
never get it at all.

Those cursed with it usually try to resist it
at first—on account of the stories—but
that never lasts long.
The Call has a way of egging you on,
invading every part of your mind until
you can’t resist the urge to pursue it.
Nowhere is safe once you've been cursed
by it, not your favorite pastime, not your
lover's arms, and not even your dreams.
It becomes an obsession; one deep enough
to completely change a person from a
right, good woman, into a stone faced
killer.
Yes… The tower is truly the scariest thing
about the forest.

The Cabin In The Forest 3
I could feel the air in the cabin grow
heavier as she finished her story. The
kindling fire in the room seemed to growl
once again.
“The tower, huh?” The grayed man
began. His mouth moved oddly, as if the
words tasted bitter on his tongue.
“Ain’t too much good can come from that,
everyone who goes after it ends up dead…
”
or worse…
The red haired woman’s lip curled in
defiance as she exhaled through her
nostrils. Her eyes never left her ax.
“Not everyone,
” the old lady exclaimed
with a shaky tone.
“My granddaughter,
she used to speak about it all the time. I
know she’s still—
”

“Elk crap!” The old man’s wicked laugh
had returned.
“There ain’t no way a girl
barely old enough to get her first monthly
is surviving in that fog alone.
”
The old woman’s eyes shot to him with
fury as his rant continued.
“I mean ya just heard the red head, if the
fog ain’t get her then a mountain li—
”
The old woman was fast. Before anyone
could even react, she had grabbed one of
the mustached man’s crossbow bolts and
raised it to the grayed man’s throat.
“Hey now hold on!” began the mustached
man as he raised quickly to his feet.
“if we
don’t all settle down we’re gonna end up
attractin—
“

“
—Speak ill of my granddaughter one
more time, and I promise it’ll never
happen again!”
The old man smiled nervously. Sweat
drenched his brow as he began to speak.
“Alright, alright point taken. It won’t
happen again.
” He laughed.
Before the tension could settle, the red
haired woman was up. Her face cocked
awkwardly to the side as she pressed her
head to the cabin wall.
We all grew quiet, we knew what that
meant; danger.
A low growling started outside of the
cabin.
Low at first; then louder.
The red haired woman readied her ax at
her waist.

The mustached man loaded his crossbow.
Everyone crouched lower.
Beastly growling continued, eerily circling
the cabin as it grew. Whatever horrid
creature out there was hungry.
We stayed like that, quiet and unmoving,
for some time; maybe 10, 20 minutes. 20
long minutes of fear filled stares into each
other’s eyes.
The grayed man’s eyes were the most
interesting. They were almost as lifeless as
my father’s had been.
“I think we’re in the clear,
” the mustached
man began.
“It’s most likely moved on by
”
now.
Everyone relaxed, only slightly, as we
continued to speak in hushed voices.

“How much longer until sunrise?” I asked.
My voice shook. I hadn’t realized how
scared I’d truly been this entire time.
“About an hour and a half left,
” answered
the old lady. That was fine, I could surely
last for that long, right?
“Ok, everybody,
” the man with the
mustache spoke at his normal volume,
“how about we all gather round again and
calm down, the danger’s gone.
”
“For now,
” the grayed man retorted.
He was right.
“Well, uh yes for now,
” he cleared his
throat awkwardly.
“As I was sayin, why don’t we all gather
round again. I’ve got a tale that’s sure to
get your minds off things.
”

King Of The Forest
The man’s eyes drifted as he began. His
tone softened.
“They say that it was just before dusk on a
cool winter night. The fog was just
beginning to clear– as it does at that time–
and anyone traveling the woods could
hear It, the echoes of the red elks’ mighty
cries.
”
The man’s low voice lured us, like moths
to a flame, as he continued.
“In front of them stood the hunter; there
was always somethin’ about him that
drew intrigue.

Maybe it was the clothes that he wore—
dirty and ripped hides torn straight from
the bodies of the creatures that he hunted
out there in the fog. Maybe it was the way
that he seemed to only target those
unfortunate enough to fall to the fog’s
curse, like some benevolent protector of
the forest; or maybe it was his smell—
corrupted, sad, and bitter— like the fog
itself.
”
The grayed man’s ears perked at the
mention of the hunter; we both leaned in
closer.
“As often as the herd of red elk had
encountered the hunter, he had never
acknowledged them; this time was
different.

Ya see, the hunter had come to do what
he’d always done, but he was too late.
Anyone, anywhere in the forest that night
could feel it– the hopeless feeling of
despair that filled the air. The leader of
the herd of elk, the King, had been
changed– bitten by the black beast lying
dead at his hooves. How could the forest’s
very symbol of hope fall prey to the fog’s
corruption?”
The mustached man’s lip curled, probably
in disgust of the black beast in his story; of
course. I guess I had almost forgotten
about the hate most people held.
His story continued.
“The herd’s concerned nudges towards
The King’s left shoulder brought flashes of
the battle that had just commenced.

Their hearts paced as rhythmically as the
wind as they looked questioningly upon
him.
His eyes offered no answers, only more
concern as he peered at the hunter ahead.
For a while nothing happened; the two
just stared, hesitant to face the end of
countless symbiotic years. Tragic.
The King was the first to move, holding
his head high in declaration of an
unfaltering pride to the future he faced.
The hunter’s head followed– A silent
message of understanding.
Without a word he turned away. Just as
mysteriously as he’d appeared, the hunter
was gone. His unspoken message to The
King was clear.
‘When you can no longer
fight the corruption, I’ll be here to do
what I’ve always done.
’”

The mustached man’s story paused again.
His gaze drifted momentarily to the old
The woman exhaled loudly, preparing to
man’s window. Strange. He acted almost
speak. Her eyes never left her rusted and
as if he had known those pesky elk
bloodied ax.
personally.
She spoke slowly.
For a second I could almost hear his voice
tremble.
“The scariest thing about the forest…
”
“The King’s worn body rippled with his
own unsteady heartbeat,
” continued the
mustached man,
“He hadn’t given up to
the fog just yet, but how much longer
would he be able to withstand its grasp?
His mind raced with contemplation. What
was he to do next? If not for the worried
faces of his herd brushing affectionately
against the tuft of his neck, he could’ve
possibly stood in his own misfortune
forever. Each elk’s gentle caress held the
sweet scents of memories gone. From
their moments of stumbling legs, the herd
had been together.

Through freezing seasons and barren
times the King had been next to them, and
them next to him. They could feel his
worry.
The realization of what was next struck
them with the force of a storm-fallen tree;
their King pulled away.
His crown lifted high as he turned one
final time to the family he’d been deemed
worthy to lead. His final decree had come.
Bravely he sounded off into the night sky
one last time,
‘Live on!’
With heavy hearts and renewed
conviction their hooves tapped. As swiftly
as they’d always done, they bounded into
the forest.
”

The Cabin In The Forest 4
The mustached man’s story was
intriguing. Something about it instilled a
feeling that I hadn’t felt too often.
“I thought the elk couldn’t be corrupted
by the fog.
” I said in awe.
“Normally they can’t, but on the night of
”
a–
“
--So someone else in this little cabin’s
heard of the hunter, aye?” Interrupted the
grayed man’s voice. He spoke with
intrigue. The mustached man paused.
“Only in stories, like this one. It’s an old
story that the people of my settlement
would pass down to the young ones.
” He
looked at me and then back to the gray
haired old man.
“It was meant to teach
them that no matter what happens,
there’s always hope if you keep moving
forward.
”

“What else have you heard about the
hunter?”
“Not much, but I’m sure someone like him
can’t be real anyway, right?”
“Oh he’s real alright, as real as you and
me, as real as the fog, and as real as them
creatures out there. Him and his
brother.
”
The red haired woman’s eyes lifted
questioningly.
“Brother?”
“Yes, brother. And I’ve been looking for
them for a long time.
” His wicked laugh
returned.
“Why?” I asked as my heart began to
quicken.

He jumped sporadically to his feet, fully
engaged. The look in his eyes was of
determination. It was like he was
connecting dots in front of him that were
invisible to the rest of us.
“They say finding him and his brother is
the key!”
“The key to what?”
, the old lady asked as
she leaned in closer.
Everyone was on the edge of their seats
now.
“Everything! The key to reaching the
tower, the key to getting rid of this fog,
and the key to figuring out the forest’s
true past.
”
The red haired woman stood abruptly.

“The tower!? What more do you know
about the tower!? Tell m—
”
BANG!
The cabin door slammed open. As quickly
as it did, the red haired woman’s body
slammed to the ground. On top of her
stood a creature as black as the night.
Its four clawed legs dug deep into the
woman’s limbs. Its bear-like face growled
promises of death. Its pitch black eyes
stared coldly.
The violet fog that streamed inside of the
open door spread quickly. If we didn’t
close it soon, even more of the fog's
creatures would come in.

A fwoosh sounded as a crossbow bolt flew
through the room. The creature howled in
pain.
How had the mustached man managed to
ready his weapon so fast? Amazing; scary.
My heart thudded rapidly as I looked
around the room. The grayed man was
already making his way to close the door;
The old woman was standing in front of
me defensively, valiantly staring down the
now wounded creature.
Thoughts of my father filled my head as I
looked at them all.
Another fwoosh sounded, followed by a
squelching pop. The mustached man had
managed to land a bolt in the creature’s
left eye this time.
One bolt left.

The creature howled once again as it
recoiled backwards, blocking the grayed
man’s path to the door.
My heart thudded even louder. If only I
wasn’t so afraid, I could help somehow.
“Haaaaa” the red haired woman shouted,
barely able to lift her freshly bloodied
body off of the floor. Her trembling hands
gripped tightly around her ax’s wooden
handle.
As she raised its steel far above her head,
the mustached man’s final crossbow bolt
landed in the creature's left shoulder. Her
ax followed, flying swiftly through the
cabin air and lodging deeply into the
creature's gut.
Blood splattered violently against the
wooden walls as the creature fell.

For a second everyone stared.
No moves, no words, no breath.
Just stares.
“Close the door,
” the old woman yelled,
reminding the grayed man of his mission.
Quickly and cautiously he approached it.
The cabin’s age mocked us as it creaked
with each step that the gray haired man
made took.
Each step.
“Creeeaak!”
“Creaak! Creaak!”
Near the beast’s body...
“Creeaak!”
And...

...past the beast...
“Creaak!”
As he drew an to within arm’s length of
the door the creature jolted back up!
Its staggering limbs oozed thick blood as
red as the ax woman’s hair.
Desperation peaked as the creature let out
another deathly howl before swiftly
slinking out of the cabin.
As quickly as he could, the old man
slammed the door shut behind it.
Panic ran through everyone's faces as
they looked around.
The creature was gone, but trouble
wasn’t. The red haired woman, If she
didn’t get help soon she’d surely bleed
out.

“How long until sunrise?” I asked
frantically.
“About 30 minutes or so,
” the old lady
answered with worried eyes.
Things didn’t look good for the red head.
Even if she could survive for 30 more
minutes, she wouldn’t be able to survive a
journey through the forest, especially now
that she and the mustached man were
weaponless...
“Does anyone have any first aid,
” the
mustached man asked frantically.
“Don’t bother,
” spat the old man,
“with
wounds that deep, first aid would only be
wasted.
”

“Well, what do we do?”
“I know!” I shouted.
Everyone’s attention was on me.
“There’s one more question we should be
answering before we continue.
”
They all stared in confusion.
“And what question would that be, little
lady?”
, the man with the thick mustache
responded as he attempted to bandage the
red head’s wounds.
“Perhaps the most important question of
the night really.
” His brow wrinkled in
anticipation. His eyes cut to me.
“What happens when a group of strangers
in the forest, allows a frightened girl from
the fog inside of their cabin?”

For a while they all stared in even more
confusion. My heart raced rapidly, and
how could it not? The moment was
perfect. They were all ...defenseless.
“Well,
” I continued as their faces morphed
into utter horror at the sight of my giant
claws emerging from within the young
girl's palms.
“They all… DIE!”
